p: Sam Okafor has run the Halcyon for more than ten months, and the countdown clock says 447.
This fall the program made an uncrewed path through the window a declared option: the autonomy release is being built so the ship could fly the Breather to Mars and land it if the crew can't go.
A code assistant slipped Earth's gravity into a Mars landing routine, and the integrated sim caught it.

AR 2207 is still open, with the second test article's life test still running clean, and on the station Malik, the son of Frances Odum, who speaks for the colonists' families, has a cough that won't go away.
Now Nell Garrity of Aldergrove, the valve's maker, has asked to be paid for root cause work beyond what the fixed price contract covers, and Garrett wants them fired.
Peg Sato. Tallgrass contracts and procurement.
Quinn Abernathy. The scheduler, fast becoming Sam's right hand.
Nell Garrity. Aldergrove's account lead, the "valve lady." She brought her company's Petrel records, carried for twenty six years.
Imogen Hale. Director of the Ares Relief Authority, which owns the mission and pays for it.
Paloma Benavidez. Test engineer at Rio Puerco Electrochemical in Albuquerque, the only person who has run the Breather's stacks at Mars pressure.

Monday, November 28, 2061. 8:20 AM. Peg Sato, who read fine print for fun, had brought two coffees into Sam's office and drunk both of them while he read, and she was looking at the empty second cup as if it had let her down.

ALDERGROVE FLUID SYSTEMS PUEBLO, COLORADO NOVEMBER 23, 2061 RE: CONTRACT TA-58-0117, MAIN OXIDIZER ISOLATION VALVES. TO: TALLGRASS AEROSPACE, CONTRACTS AND PROCUREMENT.. 1. SINCE APRIL 29, 2061, ALDERGROVE HAS PROVIDED 4,800 ENGINEERING HOURS TO THE AR 2207 INVESTIGATION AT THE PROGRAM'S REQUEST. CLAUSE 14 PROVIDES 600 HOURS OF ANOMALY SUPPORT PER CONTRACT YEAR AT NO ADDITIONAL COST.. 2. WE REQUEST AN EQUITABLE ADJUSTMENT OF $1,008,000 FOR THE 4,200 HOURS ABOVE CLAUSE 14, AT OUR AUDITED 2061 RATE. RECORDS ATTACHED.. 3. THE REMAINING ROOT CAUSE WORK CAN'T BE PRICED, BECAUSE NOBODY KNOWS WHAT IT WILL FIND. WE REQUEST THAT IT BE MOVED OUT OF THE FIXED PRICE INTO A SEPARATE COST REIMBURSABLE TASK ORDER. OUR ESTIMATE THROUGH THE STAGE'S SHIPMENT IS $4.6 MILLION.. 4. ALDERGROVE WILL CONTINUE THE WORK WHILE THIS REQUEST IS CONSIDERED.. N. GARRITY, ACCOUNT LEAD

Under the letter, clipped at the corner, was the photocopy. A page of rev C cold cycle data from 2034, columns of temperatures and closing times gone soft and gray the way a copy of a copy goes. Somebody in 2034 had drawn a box around the third row in pencil. The copier had caught half of a note in the margin beside it, in a slanted hand, CYCLE 3 AFTER SO, and the rest had fallen off the edge of the glass, all but a single initial under it, W. Beside the third row, in blue ink, in the same hand as the signature on the letter: Still asking.

It's a request for equitable adjustment, Peg said. Which is the polite way to start a claim. Nobody's sued anybody. Nobody's stopped work. Paragraph four says they'll keep going while we think about it, which they didn't have to say, and which I'd like framed.

Garrett had called her at six that morning. She'd written down what he said on the back of an envelope, and she turned it around so Sam could read it. They're holding our valve hostage. Find me another supplier by Friday. I'll make the calls.

Sam read the letter a third time. The 600 hours in clause 14 had been written in 2058 by somebody who'd pictured a supplier answering a few questions on the phone, a week of an engineer's time, maybe two. Aldergrove had given the program eight times that since April, and as far as Sam knew every hour of it had gone into finding out whether a valve was going to hurt four people on their way to Mars.

Quinn knocked on the open door with the integrated plan rolled under her arm. She unrolled the departure stage's line across his desk and held the corners down with his stapler and Peg's empty cups. The stage was due to ship to the Cape in July. The valve in the letter had been inside it since September 2059. Whatever we do, she said, it happens in front of that.
Over the high bay doors the countdown clock said 447.
Ruth's Console Log, page eight: under protest.

Ruth's console log. Petrel Flow. L Minus 57 Days. April 16 2035. oh seven hundred, garrity, aldergrove, on the line. wants to hold the last flight valve 3 weeks and run the shelf valve cold in pueblo. 500 cycles. wendell's number. it was in our october risk board minutes. asks for a change order to pay for it. oh seven fifteen, contracts: firm fixed price. delivery April 30. a hold is late delivery. oh seven forty, administrator: if the valve isn't here on the 30TH we terminate for default and buy from somebody who ships. oh seven forty five, nobody else ships a 7740. everybody on the line knew it. nobody said it. me either. oh eight ten, called garrity back. told him we need it on the 30TH. he asked if i'd looked at his row 3. told him i'd looked at the schedule. oh eight eleven, that was true. April 30 1400 valve received on time. cover letter: shipped under protest. we are still asking about cycle 3. E. garrity. April 30 1430 filed the letter with the receiving papers.

I filed it with the receiving papers. I've said that sentence to an investigation board, to a staffer on the Hill, to a lawyer who was kinder about it than I'd have been, and to myself more often than to all of them put together, and it doesn't get any shorter. Emmett Garrity asked for three weeks and five hundred cold cycles on the valve that had chattered, which was exactly what Wendell had asked for in October. He asked us to pay for it, because he ran a company of four hundred people and the contract said what it said. We told him a late valve was a defaulted contract. I told him. Then I signed for his valve on the 30th and put his letter in a drawer.

I sided with the date. I want to be exact about how, because how is the useful part. Nobody on that loop thought we were gambling with a crew. We thought the fixed price had put the valve's risk on Aldergrove: their contract, their valve, their problem. A firm fixed price does move cost risk to the seller. That's all it moves. It doesn't move the consequence. When a valve doesn't close, the crew doesn't care whose ledger the valve was on.

What happened to Aldergrove afterward belongs on this page too, and I'll get to it. Page eight is R5, procurement, nearly all of it: the contract types and who carries what, the incentive arithmetic you'll be asked to do, claims and how they turn into disputes, negotiation, and how contracts end. There's B3 in it, because a contract has change control of its own, and R6, because somebody has to pay. And there's a good deal of the Code, because procurement is where good people are most tempted to treat fairness as the other side's department.
How the exam asks it. A fixed price moves cost risk to the seller. An answer that treats it as moving every risk, safety included, is a distractor.
Every contract type is an answer to one question: who pays if this costs more than we think? Line them up by how much of that risk the buyer keeps.

The fixed price family first. Firm fixed price: the seller delivers the defined scope for a set price, and if it costs more, that's the seller's loss. Buyers love it, with reason, and it only works when you can say exactly what you're buying. Fixed price incentive fee: a target cost, a target fee, a share ratio, and a ceiling the buyer won't pay above. The seller shares overruns and underruns with the buyer until the ceiling, and then carries all of it; I'll do the arithmetic in the next section. Fixed price with economic price adjustment: a fixed price that moves with something neither side controls, usually a published index for a material or for labor, named in the contract. It's for long contracts where steel or propellant or wages can move a long way in five years, and nobody wants the seller betting on inflation in its bid.

Then cost reimbursable. Cost plus fixed fee: the buyer pays the seller's allowable costs plus a fee fixed at the start. The fee doesn't change with cost, so it carries the least incentive of any type to keep cost down. It suits research where nobody can say how much effort it will take. Cost plus incentive fee: allowable costs plus a fee that moves with performance against a target cost. Under target, the seller's fee rises by its share of the savings. Over, it falls, between a minimum and a maximum. Cost plus award fee: allowable costs plus a fee the seller earns, all or in part, against written criteria for excellence in cost, schedule, and technical work, judged during the job. The criteria have to be written down and the judging has to be fair, or an award fee turns into a lever.

Time and materials sits between the two families. The buyer pays fixed hourly rates that already include the seller's profit, plus the cost of materials. It's quick to set up and right for short work you can't size yet: an emergency repair, staff to cover a gap, the first weeks of something new. Its weakness is plain, and the US government's acquisition rules say it in so many words: it provides no positive profit incentive for cost control or labor efficiency, so the buyer has to watch it. Put a not to exceed figure on it and look at the hours every month.

Those same rules list what should decide the type: how well you can define the requirement, how much price competition and cost data there are, how urgent it is, how complex, and whether the seller's accounting can support anything but a fixed price. The direction of travel is the part to remember. Unique, complex, uncertain work starts with the buyer carrying more of the risk. As a requirement recurs and the costs become known, the risk should move to the seller. And one supplier can hold more than one type: a fixed price for the part you can define, a cost type for the part you can't.

Agile work bends the question a little. When scope is supposed to move, a fixed price for fixed scope is a contract to argue about. Teams use a fixed price per sprint or per release, with time and budget fixed and the buyer's product owner choosing the scope each time; or time and materials with a cap; or a fixed price with the right to stop at the end of any sprint. The principle doesn't change. Put the risk with the party who can manage it, and write down how scope will change.

How the exam asks it. Seller's cost risk, most to least: firm fixed price first, then the other fixed price types, then T&M, then the cost types, with CPFF carrying the least. Scope you can't define points to cost reimbursable or capped T&M. Scope you can define points to fixed price.

An FPIF contract has five numbers, all agreed before the work starts. Target cost, what both sides expect the work to cost. Target fee, the seller's profit if it lands exactly on target. Target price, those two added together. Share ratio, how a difference from target is split, written buyer first, so 70/30 means the buyer takes seventy percent of any overrun or underrun and the seller thirty. And ceiling price, the most the buyer will pay whatever happens.

When the work's done, the final fee is the target fee plus the seller's share of the difference between target cost and actual cost. An underrun raises the fee and an overrun lowers it. The final price is actual cost plus final fee, unless that comes out above the ceiling, in which case it's the ceiling.

Try it. Target cost 10.0 million, target fee 1.0, target price 11.0, share 70/30, ceiling 12.0. Say the work comes in at 9.0, an underrun of 1.0. The seller keeps thirty percent of it: fee 1.0 plus 0.3 is 1.3, and the price is 9.0 plus 1.3, or 10.3. The buyer saved 0.7 against the target price, and the seller made more money by spending less, which is the whole idea. Say instead it comes in at 11.0, an overrun of 1.0. Fee 1.0 minus 0.3 is 0.7, and the price is 11.7, under the ceiling. Say it comes in at 12.0. The formula gives a fee of 1.0 minus 0.6, which is 0.4, and a price of 12.4. That's over the ceiling, so the buyer pays 12.0 and the seller's profit is zero.

Somewhere between those last two, the buyer stopped sharing. That's the point of total assumption, the cost above which the seller carries every additional dollar. To find it, take the ceiling price minus the target price, divide by the buyer's share, and add the target cost. Here that's 12.0 minus 11.0, divided by 0.7, plus 10.0, which comes to 11.43. Above 11.43 million every extra dollar of cost comes straight out of the seller's fee, and once cost passes the ceiling the seller is losing money. Between the PTA and the ceiling the seller still makes a profit, only less of it.

Why should a buyer care where the PTA sits? Because a seller whose estimate at completion has passed it has stopped sharing your risk and started carrying all of it, and people carrying all of a loss go looking for corners. Treat an estimate past the PTA as a risk trigger, and talk to them before they find the corners.

A cost plus incentive fee contract uses the same share arithmetic on the fee, with a minimum and a maximum fee where an FPIF has a ceiling price. The buyer pays every allowable cost however high it goes. So a CPIF has no point of total assumption. It has a range where the incentive works, and outside that range the seller simply gets the minimum or the maximum fee.

How the exam asks it. Final fee target fee seller's share x (target cost minus actual cost). Final price actual cost final fee, capped at the ceiling. PTA (ceiling minus target price) buyer share target cost. CPIF has a minimum and maximum fee and no PTA.

Three words get used as if they meant the same thing. A change order is a change both parties have agreed to and someone with authority has signed. A claim is one party's demand for something it believes it's owed under the contract: money, time, or a reading of the terms. The US government's disputes clause defines it as a written demand seeking, as a matter of right, the payment of money in a sum certain, the adjustment or interpretation of contract terms, or other relief. A dispute is a claim the parties haven't managed to settle.

Most claims begin the same way. Somebody on the buyer's side asks for work the contract doesn't cover, in an email or a meeting or a work order, and nobody stops to change the contract first. People call that a constructive change. The paper didn't change, and the work did. If the program asked for the work in writing, the program has usually written its own claim, and the honest response starts from there.

Claims administration is the work of handling them well. Log the claim when it arrives. Read what the contract really says. Ask for the support and check it against your own records, the work orders and logs and emails, and never against what you remember. Keep both sides working: nearly every contract requires the seller to go on performing while a claim is resolved, and a buyer who stops the work to stop the cost usually makes both of them worse. Then negotiate. Most claims settle at the table, and the early ones settle cheapest.

If they don't settle, there's a ladder, and the exam wants you on the lowest rung that works. Negotiation: the two parties, nobody else. Mediation: a neutral third person helps the parties reach their own agreement, and may propose one, but can't impose it. Arbitration: a neutral third person hears both sides and decides, and if the parties agreed in advance, the decision binds them. Mediation and arbitration are the usual forms of alternative dispute resolution, which means alternatives to court. Litigation is the top rung and the most expensive in money, in years, and in the relationship. One rule worth keeping: when two parties agree to arbitrate, they should agree in writing on the most the arbitrator can award.

A claim isn't an attack. It's the contract working. A seller who files one and keeps working is doing exactly what the contract asked of it. Treat it that way and most of them settle in a room with a pot of coffee.

How the exam asks it. Settle claims by negotiation first, then mediation or arbitration, and litigation last. The seller keeps performing while a claim is resolved. A change order is an agreed change; a claim is a request the other side hasn't agreed to yet.

In 1981 Roger Fisher and William Ury, of the Harvard Negotiation Project, wrote a short book called Getting to Yes, and its four rules are still the ones the exam assumes. Separate the people from the problem. Focus on interests, not positions. Invent options for mutual gain. Insist on objective criteria.

A position is what somebody says they want: a million dollars, a fixed price, a supplier fired. An interest is why they want it: paying sixty people in March, never being blamed again, an answer before the window. Positions usually can't both be met. Interests often can. Two sides trading positions take turns giving ground until one of them gets tired. Two sides who've put their interests on the table can look for a deal that serves both, and they're likelier to keep it once they've signed.

Before you sit down, work out your best alternative to a negotiated agreement, your BATNA: what you'll actually do if this fails. The book's own definition is the results you can obtain without negotiating. Your BATNA sets your walk away point, which some people call your reservation price. A deal worse than your BATNA is a deal to refuse. Work out theirs as well. And be honest about your own. Most managers overestimate their alternatives, because the alternative they're picturing is tidier than the one they'd get.

The zone of possible agreement is the range between the two walk away points, where any deal beats what both sides would get without one. If a buyer's alternative would cost 900 and the seller won't take less than 700, the ZOPA runs from 700 to 900, and every number in it is better for both of them than walking away. If the seller won't go below 950, there's no zone, and no amount of talking will make one. Where you land inside the zone is where objective criteria earn their keep: a market rate, an audited cost, your own records. People agree more easily to a number they can both check than to a number one of them wanted.

Two practical things. Bring the people who can say yes, or make sure your negotiator carries written authority from them, and keep everybody else off the speaker. And when your own side disagrees in front of the other party, ask for a recess and settle it in the hall. Nothing weakens a negotiating team faster than watching it argue with itself across the table.

The Code is short on this, and firm. Section 3.3.1: we negotiate in good faith. Its comment says that means working with each other honestly, openly, fairly, and with sincere motives, so the other party can receive the benefits it agreed to. A bluff about an alternative you don't have is a statement designed to deceive, and 5.3.1 rules it out. You don't have to show anyone your walk away point. You can't invent one.

How the exam asks it. Negotiate interests, know your BATNA before you start, and settle on objective criteria. A deal outside the ZOPA leaves one side worse off than no deal. Bluffs, threats, and splitting the difference by reflex are distractors.
Most contracts end by being finished: delivered, accepted, paid, and closed. The ones that end early end one of two ways, and the difference matters more than people expect.

Termination for convenience is the buyer's right, written into the contract, to end it for the buyer's own reasons: the need went away, or the money did, or the plan changed. The seller isn't at fault, so the seller is paid for the work it has done and the reasonable costs of stopping, with a fair profit on the work done, though not on work it never gets to do.

Termination for default is for a seller that has failed to perform. It didn't deliver on time, or it isn't making progress and the contract is in danger, or it broke another of the terms. If the seller isn't making progress or has broken another term, the buyer usually has to give written notice and a chance to cure, often ten days. A missed delivery date can be grounds on its own. A seller terminated for default may be paid nothing for undelivered work and can owe the buyer the extra cost of buying it elsewhere. That's why the bar is high. And if it turns out afterward that the seller wasn't in default, or that its failure came from causes it couldn't control, the termination is treated as one for convenience, and the buyer pays as if it had chosen to end the contract all along.

In September 2035, three months after June 12, the agency terminated every contract Aldergrove had with it for default. Their valve had met every requirement the contract set. It was the requirement that hadn't been good enough, and the requirement was ours. In 2039 an appeals board said so. The terminations became terminations for convenience, and Aldergrove was paid its costs. By then it had sixty one people. A wrongful default costs the buyer the money anyway, and it can cost the seller everything else.

So before anybody terminates a supplier, count what goes with it. The money is the smallest part. You lose the people who know the part. You start qualification over. You teach every supplier you'll ever have what happens to the ones who bring you bad news. Emmett Garrity wrote to the investigation board every June after that, one page, with a copy of his cold cycle data clipped to it. I was on the distribution until the board was dissolved. I didn't answer one of them.

How the exam asks it. For convenience: the buyer's choice, and the seller is paid for work done. For default: the seller's failure, usually after a cure notice. A default termination that turns out to be wrongful is treated as one for convenience.

The make or buy decision comes before all of this: produce it ourselves, or buy it? The analysis compares the full cost of each over the quantity you need, direct and indirect, and then the things that won't fit in a spreadsheet cell. Do you have the skill, the capacity, and the time? Does the work expose your intellectual property, or theirs? Do you want the capability afterward? Leave sunk costs out. Money already spent on a line or a building is gone whichever way you decide, so it can't be a reason to decide.

The arithmetic is a breakeven. Making usually means a fixed cost to set up and a variable cost per unit. Buying usually means a price per unit. The breakeven quantity is the fixed cost divided by the difference between the buy price per unit and the make cost per unit. Below the breakeven, buying is cheaper; above it, making is, if everything else is equal, which it rarely is. If tooling costs 400 and each unit costs 3 to make or 5 to buy, the breakeven is 400 divided by 2, or 200 units.

Once the contract's signed, the supplier is part of your project, and you manage it like one. Agree how performance will be measured and review it with them on a schedule. Check that what's delivered meets the contract's acceptance criteria before you pay for it. Keep the records: the contract, every change, every invoice, every inspection, every letter. A procurement audit will ask for them one day, and so will whoever has your job after you.

A supplier also opens a door into your systems, and people who steal for a living know it. The oldest trick is an email that looks like it's from the supplier's finance office, sent the week an invoice is due, asking you to pay a new bank account. Treat IT security as a risk like any other. It goes in the risk register with an owner, a trigger, and a response: confirm every payment change by phone to a number you already had, give each supplier only the access its work needs, and take that access back the day the work ends. When an attempt does reach someone's inbox, that's the trigger firing. Log it, tell the owner, and keep the email.

A contract has its own change control. Only the person with contracting authority can change it, in writing, through the clause the contract names. That sits alongside the program's change board. The board decides whether the program wants the change and what it does to cost, schedule, scope, and risk; the person with contracting authority makes it binding. Do both, in that order, and update the plan when it's signed. On a cost type contract it matters even more. When the buyer pays the cost, new work is tempted to slide in without a change, and the target the incentive was built on stops meaning anything.

How the exam asks it. Ignore sunk costs. Verify deliverables before payment. An IT security threat, like a phishing email asking to change a supplier's bank details, is a risk: log it with an owner and a response, and verify by a channel you already trust. Contract changes go through the project's change control and are made binding only by the person with contracting authority.

The Code defines fairness as our duty to make decisions and act impartially and objectively, with conduct free from competing self-interest, prejudice, and favoritism. In procurement it gets specific. 4.2.1: transparency in our decision making. 4.2.3: equal access to information for those authorized to have it, which in a bid means every bidder gets the same answers. 4.3.1 and 4.3.2: disclose any real or potential conflict of interest to the appropriate stakeholders, and stay out of the decision until it's disclosed, there's an approved plan to manage it, and they've agreed. The comment adds that we treat the appearance of a conflict as a conflict. And 4.3.3: we don't award or deny contracts on personal considerations, including favoritism, nepotism, or bribery.

Add 3.3.4, which says we respect the property rights of others and counts data and intellectual property as property, so a supplier's proprietary data isn't yours because it happens to be useful. And 3.3.2: we don't exercise the power of our expertise or position to influence the decisions or actions of others in order to benefit personally at their expense. A buyer squeezing a supplier is usually doing it for the company, not for himself, so 3.3.2 doesn't often settle it. Good faith does. Under 3.3.1 the other side has to be able to receive the benefits it agreed to, and fairness, back where this section started, means deciding impartially and objectively. A buyer with a small supplier over a barrel holds real power, and the temptation to use it doesn't feel like a temptation. It feels like a good deal.
That's page eight. I filed the letter. When one comes to you, answer it.

How the exam asks it. A conflict of interest is disclosed, and the person steps back from the decision. Steering work to a friend, a relative, or an investor's company without disclosure is a violation even when the price is good.

Tuesday, November 29. 7:30 AM. Peg had spent the evening with the contract, all two hundred and twelve pages of it, and had come in with eleven sticky flags along its edge in four colors, which she said was a system.

There was no second test article The root cause team was working from the archive the April data and a cold bench Aldergrove's engineers had built in Pueblo out of spare parts and stubbornness Either way, nobody on the team said soon anymore.

Clause 14 is six hundred hours a year, Peg said. Whatever paper anybody signed in the spring, none of it says four thousand eight hundred. And here's the part Garrett won't like. We asked for those hours. Hana's team sent them work orders. Some of the work orders have your initials on them.

Garrett had already called legal. Legal had a two paragraph reply drafted by nine: the contract is firm fixed price, clause 14 is the limit, the request is denied. Hana had read it over Peg's shoulder and put it down on the table face first. If their people walk, half my root cause team walks with them. They're the only engineers alive who've built a 7740.
Aldergrove is claiming far more than clause 14 allows, and legal has a denial drafted. What should Sam do?
A. Have legal send the drafted denial today, citing the firm fixed price and clause 14's limit.
B. Ask Aldergrove to put the root cause work on hold until Peg and Nell have settled the claim.
C. Log the letter as a claim, and have Peg check its hours against the program's own work orders.
D. Pay the full request now, and have Peg sort out the contract paperwork with Aldergrove next month.

Peg logs it in the contract file as CL-0012 and writes to Aldergrove for the hour records, by work order. Sam calls Pueblo at noon. Nell Garrity, Aldergrove's account lead, answers on the first ring, which he notices. Thank you for calling instead of writing. She tells him the past hours matter less to her than the next six months. I can't give you a fixed price for finding out something nobody knows. If I make one up, I'm either robbing you or I'm going to stop looking when the money runs out. I won't do either one. By Friday Peg has the count. Thirty six hundred of the hours tie to work orders the program wrote. Six hundred were Aldergrove scanning its own archive, which helped everybody, and which Aldergrove had decided to do on its own.

That's a go. Claims administration starts with treating the claim as what it is, a request under the contract that deserves a review. Document it, verify its basis against your own records, keep the work going, and talk to the person behind the letter before the positions harden.
Thursday, December 1. 7:00 AM. Garrett was in the big room before anyone else, with a single page on the table and his reading glasses on top of it.
KESTREL FLOW CONTROLS COLORADO SPRINGS LETTER OF INTEREST. KESTREL CAN DELIVER A QUALIFIED CRYOGENIC ISOLATION VALVE FOR THE HALCYON DEPARTURE STAGE BY MAY 2062. FIRM FIXED PRICE. WE DON'T DO CLAIMS.
Garrett had heard about the claim on Monday and had been making calls ever since, as he'd said he would.
Fixed price, he said, tapping the page. No claims. They're hungry and they're an hour and a half down the road. Terminate Aldergrove, Peg drafts it today, and we're done being held hostage.
Hana read the page twice. Qualified to what? How many times has a Kestrel valve closed after a cold soak at this size? I'll tell you. None. Ours is already in the stage.

Peg didn't say anything in the meeting. Afterward she came to Sam's office with a printout from the state's business filings. Kestrel's board chair was a man who also sat on Tallgrass's investor board, which had met on November 15. Garrett hadn't mentioned it.
Garrett wants to move the valve work to Kestrel. What's Sam's best move?
A. Back Garrett's plan, and have Peg draft a notice moving the valve contract to Kestrel.
B. Keep Aldergrove, and start qualifying Kestrel's valve as a second source in parallel.
C. Assess the switch as a risk with Quinn and Hana, and put Kestrel's investor tie on record.
D. Send Aldergrove a letter warning of termination for default, as leverage on the claim.

Quinn and Hana have the comparison by four. Kestrel's valve has never closed cold at this size. Replacing the installed valve means destacking, a new qualification of at least seven months, and a second acceptance firing, and the stage misses its slot at the Cape and the window behind it. Peg adds the contract side: Aldergrove isn't in default, and a wrongful default becomes a termination for convenience, so the program would pay Aldergrove's costs and lose its engineers too. Sam writes it into the risk register as R-0517, claim unresolved with the sole qualified supplier, response mitigate, by negotiation. At the bottom of the page is one more line: Kestrel's board chair sits on Tallgrass's investor board. Sam sends it to Garrett first, alone. Garrett calls him in eleven minutes. You think I'd put a valve on a ship for a friend? No, sir, Sam says. I think the change board should know, so nobody else has to wonder. A long pause. Fine. Put it in. On Wednesday the board records it with a mitigation: any decision involving Kestrel comes to the board without Garrett's vote, and Garrett agrees.

Good. That's what I'd want on my loop. Assess a supplier switch as a risk decision, with data: qualification, schedule, and the people who know the part. Termination needs grounds and has consequences. A link between a decision maker and a bidder is a conflict of interest to disclose (Code 4.3.1), whoever holds it.
Monday, December 5. Peg had divided the big room whiteboard down the middle with a line of blue tape. On the left, in her capitals, WHAT WE KNOW. On the right, WHAT WE DON'T.

The left side was short. The valve was a 7740 rev F. It had one real event on record, 40 milliseconds, the third close after a cold soak. Nobody had been able to make it do it again. The right side ran down to the floor. Why. How many cycles. Whether the answer needed a teardown. Whether there would be a fix, and what it would cost, and who would build it.

Aldergrove's estimate for the remaining work was $4.6 million, and Nell had said on the phone that $0.6 million of it was Aldergrove's own contingency, because a supplier quoting the unknowable pads the quote.

Peg had three drafts on the table, a fixed price, time and materials with a cap, and cost plus incentive fee. Garrett's assistant had forwarded a fourth that morning: cost plus award fee, with the award decided each quarter by the office of the CEO.

Hana stood at the right side of the board with a marker she hadn't used yet. Whatever we sign, she said, has to pay them to find the answer. It can't pay them to stop looking, and it can't pay them to look forever.
Peg has three contract drafts, and Garrett's office sent a fourth. Which one should Sam pick?
A. A firm fixed price for the remaining root cause work, set at Aldergrove's own estimate.
B. Cost plus award fee, with the award set each quarter by the office of the CEO.
C. Time and materials at Aldergrove's audited rates, with a not to exceed cap and monthly review.
D. Cost plus incentive fee, with a target cost and a fee that rises as cost comes in under it.

Peg drafts it at the table and Nell redlines it by phone the same afternoon. Target cost $4.0 million, which is Aldergrove's estimate with its own contingency taken out, because a cost type contract doesn't need it. Target fee eight percent, $320,000. Share 80/20, buyer first. Minimum fee $120,000, maximum $520,000. Deliverables by the month: a data package to the root cause team, a status to the board's clerk, and, when there is one, a root cause report. Peg checks the one thing the rules say to check first. Aldergrove's accounting system was audited for cost type work in 2059, and it passed. Hana reads the draft and finally uses her marker, on the right side of the board, under WHY. It pays them to look efficiently, she says. It doesn't pay them to stop.

Exactly right. When the scope can't be defined, a cost reimbursable contract fits, and an incentive fee gives the seller a reason to control cost. Define the deliverables and the fee formula up front, and confirm the seller can account for costs before you sign.

Wednesday, December 7. The program's change board met at two, as it did every Wednesday, in the big room with the integrated plan on the wall and a plate of somebody's cookies going stale in the middle of the table.

The first item on the agenda was Aldergrove: settle the past hours, and move the remaining root cause work out of the fixed price into a separate task order, cost plus incentive fee, as drafted on Monday.

At 1:40 Garrett called Peg directly. You've got signing authority to ten million. Sign it. I don't need a committee looking at my supplier. Peg had the authority. She'd been given it in writing in 2057 and had it framed, next to a drawing her nephew had made of a dragon.
She came to the board anyway, with the modification in a folder, and sat down beside Sam. I can sign this, she said quietly. The question is whether I should yet.
Garrett tells Peg to sign the modification today. What should Sam do?
A. Take the modification to the change board and hold Peg's signature until it's approved.
B. Cover the new work in a side letter with Aldergrove, and fold it into the contract later.
C. Have Peg sign the modification under her own authority, and report it to the board next week.
D. Ask Garrett to approve the modification as CEO in place of a change board review.

CR-0388 goes up at two. What changes in the contract. Where the money comes from: contingency, from the line AR 2207 has had since June. What it does to the root cause schedule and to the stage's ship date, which is nothing, if the work keeps going. What it does to the risk register: R-0517 down a notch, a new one for a cost type contract the program has never managed before. The board approves the structure, sets the limits Sam and Peg will carry into the negotiation, and records the decision with the reasons. Quinn updates the plan before the cookies are gone. Peg puts the unsigned modification back in her folder. After Pueblo, she says. Then it'll mean something.

That's a go. A contract change is a project change. Assess its effect on cost, schedule, scope, and risk through integrated change control and record the decision, and then the person with contracting authority signs it and the documents get updated.
Friday, December 9. The meeting was set for Wednesday the 14th, at ten, at Aldergrove's plant on the south side of Pueblo. Aldergrove would bring its president, Nell, and its lawyer.

Garrett wanted to lead it. CEO to CEO. They'll want to see the man who signs. Tallgrass's legal office wanted to send two lawyers and keep it formal. Hana had already cleared the day. Gwen Talley, Hale's chief of staff, had called to ask, carefully, whether the ARA should know anything before Wednesday, since the ARA would be the one explaining any of it to the board and the partners.
Peg had made a list of who could go and what each of them would change by being in the room. She'd written GARRETT at the top and then, beside it in smaller letters, phone.
Everyone wants a seat at Wednesday's meeting with Aldergrove. How should Sam staff it?
A. Send Tallgrass's lawyers to run the meeting on the contract's terms with Peg in support.
B. Send Peg to lead it, carrying spending limits that Garrett signs before Wednesday.
C. Drive to Pueblo first and settle it with Nell himself, then have Peg write up what they agree.
D. Let Garrett lead the meeting CEO to CEO, with Peg and Sam beside him at the table.

Garrett signs the limits on Monday morning after Peg walks him through the work orders: up to $1.0 million on the past hours, and the task order as the board approved it. He agrees to be on his phone in Denver at 10:30 for a check in. Sam calls Gwen that afternoon with what the program is going to ask for, why, and what it would mean for the board's AR 2207 data, which is that the board would get more of it. The Director likes hearing it before rather than after, she says. Tell us how it ends, the same day. Hana spends the weekend making a single page of what the root cause team needs from Aldergrove through the summer, in order.

Good. That's what I'd want on my loop. Engaging stakeholders means deciding who participates, in what role, and with what authority, and keeping the people affected informed. Put the person who knows the contract at the table with written limits, keep the decision maker reachable, and brief the sponsor before the meeting.
Monday, December 12. Peg ran the prep session in the big room with the door shut: Sam, Hana, Quinn, and a yellow legal pad she'd divided into columns with a ruler.

The first column was POSITIONS. Aldergrove: $1,008,000 for the past hours, and a cost type contract for the rest. Tallgrass legal: nothing for the past hours, and the fixed price stands. She read them both out and then drew a line under them.

Those are positions, she said. I don't negotiate positions. I negotiate what's under them. If we go down there and trade numbers, we'll end up halfway between two numbers nobody believes, and we'll all feel very grown up about it.
Garrett's text arrived at 10:15, to Peg and Sam. Open at 200K. Tell them Kestrel is ready. It works.
Peg turned the pad to a clean page.
Peg is running the prep session, and Garrett's text says open at 200K. How should they prepare?
A. Prepare a generous list of concessions, and skip working out what happens without a deal.
B. Agree in advance to offer a split down the middle between the two opening positions.
C. Work out each side's interests and walk away point, and the standard both could check.
D. Prepare the legal case in detail, from clause 14 and the work orders to what each side can prove.

The pad fills up. Aldergrove's interests: being paid for work done, a contract that doesn't punish it for finding the answer, cash in March for sixty people, and the truth about cycle 3. Tallgrass's: the root cause before the stage ships, cost it can explain to an auditor, and Aldergrove's engineers still at the table in June. Then the alternatives, with numbers, which Quinn checks twice. If there's no deal, the claim goes to arbitration; Peg's estimate of what that would cost Tallgrass, and of what it would net Aldergrove, gives each side's walk away point and a wide zone between them. Then the standard: the program's own work orders. Thirty six hundred hours at Aldergrove's audited rate is $864,000. It sits inside the zone. Nobody has to win that number, she says. It's ours, and it's true. Then she picks up her phone and answers Garrett's text with one word. No.

Exactly right. Prepare a negotiation on interests, not positions: know both sides' alternatives, find the zone where an agreement beats both, and bring an objective standard. A bluff about an alternative is dishonest, and it's also bad preparation.

Wednesday, December 14. Pueblo. They drove down I-25 in the dark and got there early. Aldergrove's plant was a long brick building on the south side with a newer metal one bolted to its end, and the conference room was upstairs in the old part, with a window that looked straight across the road at the steel mill: a long brown shed with steam rising from one end, rail cars stacked with pipe, and a crane that never seemed to move until you looked away and back.

Aldergrove's president was a big quiet man in his sixties with a notebook he didn't open. Their lawyer was a woman with a laptop she did. Nell, who'd written the letter, sat at the end of the table nearest the window with a folder in front of her and the old steel badge on its lanyard that Sam had noticed in April.

Peg opened with interests, theirs and Tallgrass's, in that order, and asked whether she'd got Aldergrove's right. The president corrected one of them and added another. For forty minutes it went the way the yellow pad had said it might.

At 10:30 Peg's phone lit up and she put Garrett on speaker, as agreed, for his check in. He listened for about a minute. Then he said, in the warm voice he used on investors: Let me be clear, folks. Tallgrass has options. Kestrel can have a valve in Watkins by May. If Aldergrove wants to play claims, we can play contracts.
Nobody said anything. Aldergrove's lawyer started typing. The president closed his notebook, which he hadn't opened. Nell turned and looked out of the window at the mill.
Garrett just threatened Aldergrove over the speaker. What should Sam do now?
A. Correct Garrett on the speaker in front of Aldergrove, and make clear that Peg speaks for Tallgrass.
B. End the session politely, and propose meeting again in January once Tallgrass has one position.
C. Let Garrett's statement about Kestrel stand, and use it to bring Aldergrove's number down.
D. Ask for a short recess, and take Garrett off speaker in the hall to settle who speaks.

Let's take fifteen minutes, Peg says, and the president nods like a man who's done this before. In the hall by a vending machine Sam takes the phone off speaker. They need to know we're not soft. They know what we can do, sir, Sam says. They also know the valve's already in the stage and Kestrel can't do May. Every time somebody from our side says it, they hear 2035. Peg, beside him, says nothing, on purpose. You signed Peg's limits on Monday. Either they hold, or I drive home and you come down here yourself. A long silence on the line. They hold. Take me off the dial in. Back in the room Peg says one sentence. Mr. Lyle wanted you to know how seriously Tallgrass takes this. I speak for Tallgrass today. The president opens his notebook.

That's a go. When your own side's conflict surfaces in front of the other party, take it offline. Assess it, approach the person directly and privately (Code 3.2.7), settle who has authority, and come back with one voice.

During the recess Nell didn't go for coffee. She stood at the window with her arms folded and looked at the mill, and after a minute Sam went and stood beside her, because it seemed she'd wanted somebody to.

My father used to bring me up here on Saturdays when I was a kid, she said. This was his office, before it was a conference room. He liked to watch the mill. He said it was the only thing in Pueblo that worked harder than he did. She turned the steel badge on its lanyard so he could read it. It wasn't her name. E. GARRITY. PRESIDENT.

The agency terminated us for default in September of 2035. Every contract we had with them, the same week. We had four hundred and ten people. By 2037 we had sixty one. It took an appeals board four years to say we hadn't been in default, that the valve met everything the contract asked of it. They changed it to a termination for convenience and paid us our costs, and nobody put that in the paper. By then it was 2039 and he was the man who'd killed the Petrel, in every bar on this side of town.

He wrote to the investigation board every June twelfth. One page, and that page you've got, the copy clipped to it. We're still asking about cycle three. W was Wendell Price. You've worked that out. My father meant to call him in 2034 and didn't, because by then Wendell was the agency's man, and you didn't call the agency's people. Nobody ever wrote back.

She looked at the end of the table, where Aldergrove's president had left his notebook. He died at his desk in March of 2041. That desk, they kept it. His heart, the doctor said. He was sixty three. He'd already written that year's letter. It was in the drawer with the copy clipped to it, and I mailed it in June, and I've mailed one every June since, to whoever has the Mars work. This year it's you. I didn't want to wait till June.

So you should know why I wrote the claim. We need the money. We're sixty people. That's real, and it's not why. The Petrel killed my father, Mr. Okafor. It took six years to do it. I won't ship a valve I don't trust, for a fixed price or for anything else, and I'd rather be fired than be asked to. A breath. I'd rather you didn't fire me.

They went back to the table. Aldergrove's president restated it plainly: $1,008,000 for the past hours, and the task order for the rest. Peg had her pad face down in front of her. Garrett's signed limit on the past hours was $1.0 million. The program's own work orders came to $864,000.
Aldergrove wants $1,008,000 for the past hours. What should Sam agree to pay?
A. Settle the past hours at $864,000 from the work orders, and sign the incentive fee task order.
B. Accept the full $1,008,000 with Garrett's approval by phone, and sign the task order at their estimate.
C. Meet Aldergrove halfway at $936,000 for the past hours, and sign the incentive fee task order.
D. Offer $490,000 for the past hours, near their walk away point, and say Kestrel is ready if they refuse.

Peg turns the pad over and walks the president through the work orders, one by one. The six hundred archive hours were Aldergrove's choice, and he says so before she has to. They shake on $864,000 at a quarter to one. The task order goes as drafted: target cost $4.0 million, eight percent target fee, 80/20, the fee floor and cap, the monthly data package, and every finding shared with the readiness board with Aldergrove credited by name. Nell asks for one thing more, and Peg writes it into the statement of work in her own words before anyone can argue: Deliverable 1: an answer to the question Aldergrove has asked every June since 2036 about cycle 3 after a cold soak, or a written statement of why there isn't one yet. Nell reads it twice. He'd have liked that, she says. He'd have said it was badly punctuated.

Good. That's what I'd want on my loop. Principled negotiation settles on an objective standard both sides can check, here the program's own records, and builds the agreement around both sides' interests. Inside the zone of agreement, the fair number and the durable number are usually the same one.
Decision nine. Where it comes from.

Monday, December 19. The settlement had come to $864,000, and the new task order had a target price of its own. In June the program had set aside money inside its contingency for AR 2207's future costs, Aldergrove's support among them. Quinn had it all on one page with the gap circled: about $3.3 million more than the June line.

Garrett had a suggestion, which he made in the hallway, which was where he made the suggestions he didn't want minuted. The Breather fabrication account has room this quarter. Charge it there. The valve line won't show a thing.

At 11 Calvin Osterhout, the ARA's comptroller, called from Washington. He'd seen the board's notice of a new cost type task order and he had two questions, which he asked in the order he cared about them. Where's the money coming from? And does the number I give the partners move?
The program's estimate at completion was 2,600, the number the Rule 4.2 notice had carried since July, against a budget of 2,472. The partners were still taking up the October quarterly.
Calvin asks where the money's coming from, and whether his number moves. How should Sam answer?
A. Draw it from the contingency set aside for AR 2207, and update the estimate at completion.
B. Ask Director Hale to release management reserve for the settlement and the new task order.
C. Charge the new costs to the Breather fabrication account, which has room this quarter.
D. Leave the forecast where it is until the first invoice under the new task order arrives.

Quinn moves the money on Tuesday and writes down where it came from: the settlement and the task order's target price, out of contingency, against the AR 2207 line and then the general pool for the rest. She works the estimate at completion again. The July bottom up had carried an allowance for most of it, so the bottom up stays about 2,600, and she shows the Aldergrove line on its own row so anyone can see it. She adds the one thing a cost type contract changes: there's no ceiling, so the estimate has a range, and she shows it. Sam calls Calvin back at four with all of it. There's a pause on the line. That's the first time this year anyone's told me where money came from before I had to ask, he says. I'll fight you on the next one anyway.

Exactly right. Pay for an identified risk from the contingency held for it, record the draw, update the forecast, and report it through governance with the source. Management reserve waits for what nobody saw coming.
Decision ten. Nothing on the shelf.

Sunday, December 25. Christmas. Sam hadn't put up a tree. He'd hung Grace's red glass pepper on the knob of the cabinet over the coffee maker, where Ada would have put it at the very top, and at eight he sat at the kitchen table and recorded a log, and watched it back, and it was the voice the whole way through, cheerful, every sentence. He didn't send it. The last time he'd seen her without a screen between them was at the crew bus at the Cape, in the dark, in December of 2058. She'd said she'd log every week. He'd said, Your mother would never have let you go. She'd looked at him for a second, and then she'd got on the bus. She'd logged every week since. Neither of them had brought it up. On Friday he sent a short one about Pueblo instead.
Tuesday, January 3, 2062. 5:40 AM. The two note chime.

A log from Ada Okafor, Ares Station. Sol 3866. One way, 16 minutes 53 seconds. Margin, 602 days. Hi, Dad. Log one. I'm numbering them now. Comms says that in the weeks around conjunction some packets don't get through, and the ones that do come in out of order. So from now on every log has a number, and if you get eleven and then thirteen, you'll know there was a twelve, and you'll know I sent it. You'll want to fill it in. Don't. Just know it was there. Christmas was good. We had one. Bay A made a tree out of a trellis and forty empty seed packets on strings, and Malik climbed it to put a star on top, which was a sample tube with foil on it, and he only coughed twice, and medical found two of the good inhalers in a kit from '57 behind a panel nobody had opened in years, and gave him one, and he carries it around like a medal. You didn't send one for Christmas. That's okay. I think you recorded one. You always record one and then sit there deciding, and I can see you deciding from here, which is three hundred million kilometers, I looked it up. Your Friday one was short. You said Pueblo four times. You didn't say anything about the valve lady except that she has a view of a steel mill, so something happened, and it's hers, and okay. Now the thing. I should have told you this a long time ago, and I didn't, because I thought it was the kind of thing a director tells his agency and not the kind of thing a daughter tells her dad. The spare stacks are gone. All six. Hollis's weekly says six RP-55 stacks in stores. They're not in stores. They're in the plant. The first one went in more than a year ago. The last one went in three weeks before you got the ship. Every time one of the old stacks quit, we put a spare in, and the stores list never changed, because taking a stack off it is a form, and the form goes to Earth, and nobody wanted to be the one who sent it. So it's still on the page every Monday. Six spares. There's nothing on the shelf, Dad. I went and looked. There's a shelf. My number has always been the plant with all six already in it. The agency's model puts them in this year. That's most of your sixty days. I'm sorry I didn't say. I thought it was his to say. He hasn't, and I don't think he's going to, and the people building the thing that's supposed to replace this plant should know the old one has nothing left in its pockets. I watched yours twice. You looked tired. You only look tired when you're telling me everything. 602. Same minus nine. Love you. Log one. Ada out.
He watched it twice. The second time he stopped it on the shelf, and on her hand flat against it.

At 7:10 he put one question into the morning packet for the joint Breather team, the routine way, as part of the cutover inventory the plan needed anyway: Q2: Station stores count of RP-55 stacks, by serial. The answer came back the next morning, at the end of the station's shift, from Chiamaka Okonkwo, who led Breather operations on the station and answered exactly what she was asked.

JOINT BREATHER TEAM MORNING PACKET SOL 3867 ANSWERS FROM C. OKONKWO, BREATHER OPERATIONS. Q2, UNDERSTOOD AS: HOW MANY RP-55 STACKS ARE IN STATION STORES, BY SERIAL, FOR THE CUTOVER INVENTORY.. A2: NONE IN STORES. SERIALS 55-0441 TO 55-0446 ARE ALL INSTALLED IN THE PLANT. PLANT LOG REFERENCES ATTACHED. THE STORES LIST WAS NOT UPDATED. A CORRECTION HAS GONE TO THE DIRECTOR FOR SIGNATURE.. Q3 FROM US: DOES THE CUTOVER PLAN ASSUME STORES SPARES? IF IT DOES, WHO DECIDES WHAT REPLACES THEM?
The packet went where all the packets went, to the joint team and to the ARA's mission assurance office, which read every one.

It did assume them. Quinn found the line in the cutover plan in four minutes: during the forty sols it would take to install and start the Breather, the old plant would keep the station breathing, and if one of its stacks quit, the station would put in a spare from stores. The risk register said the same thing in different words. So did the ARA's own margin model, which credited six spares going into the plant in 2062.
The station's stores have none of the spare stacks everyone counts on. How should Sam respond?
A. Pass the stores gap to the ARA's station operations office as the owner of the spares.
B. Have Quinn trace the stores gap through every part of the integrated plan it touches.
C. Ask Rio Puerco for a quote on six RP-55 stacks today, and open the procurement file.
D. Keep the stores news inside the program until replacement stacks are on order.

It takes two days. Quinn rewrites the cutover plan around six bridge stacks flown on Halcyon. Hana weighs them, 430 kilograms with mounts, against the cargo module's margin and the propellant behind it, and it fits, with less left over than she likes. The risk register's response for a stack failure during cutover changes from station spares to VOID, in capitals, and a new risk takes its place. Peg starts a procurement file. The funding goes to the ARA as a change request, because the stacks are station property replacing the station's own spares. And Sam writes to the board's clerk and Hale's office about the margin, citing Chiamaka's packet and the plant log, and nothing else: the ARA's model credits six spare stacks that were installed in 2060, and the board may want to check it. Hale calls at six. Sixty days? About that, ma'am. The board should check it. Not me. She's quiet for a while. Then the board will have it by Friday.

That's a go. A new fact that touches several plans is an integration problem. Assess it across the integrated plan, update the subsidiary plans and the risk register together, and report what governance needs to know through the right channel, from the record.
Monday, January 9. One way or another, the program had to buy six RP-55 stacks, and they had to be in Watkins by May 15 to make the cargo module's manifest closeout on June 1.

Rio Puerco had built the station's plant in 2055. Paloma Benavidez, their test engineer, called from Albuquerque at eight with her safety glasses on her head and a stack of old binders behind her. I ran RP-55 acceptance my first year here. I was twenty eight. The tooling's in the back of Building 3 under a tarp with my handwriting on it. Rio Puerco's offer was an incentive contract: target cost $12.0 million, target fee $1.2 million, target price $13.2 million, share 80/20, ceiling $14.4 million. Or a firm fixed price of $15.1 million, which Paloma said, without being asked, was the same work with the line's restart risk priced in.

Garrett wanted to build them at Watkins. We've got a stack assembly line. It's paid for. We keep the capability. Quinn had the numbers for that too. Restarting an RP-55 line at Tallgrass meant new tooling, a requalification of a design nobody there had touched, and training: $5.0 million fixed, then about $1.6 million a stack. And Tallgrass's stack assembly line was the Breather's critical path, which it had been since March.
Rio Puerco makes two offers, and Garrett wants to build at Watkins. How should the six stacks be sourced?
A. Buy from Rio Puerco at its firm fixed price of $15.1 million, with the risk on the seller.
B. Buy from Rio Puerco on the incentive contract, with its 80/20 share and $14.4 million ceiling.
C. Build the stacks on Tallgrass's own assembly line, which is already paid for.
D. Put the stacks out for competitive bids from three electrochemical suppliers over six weeks.

Quinn does the comparison in front of everybody. Making six costs $5.0 million plus $9.6 million, $14.6 million, and takes the Breather's critical path to do it. Buying at target costs $13.2 million, and even at the ceiling, $14.4 million, it's cheaper than making. The line Garrett says is paid for is paid for either way. Peg checks the share and the ceiling, works out where Rio Puerco stops sharing, and writes it on the file as a number to watch. The contract is signed on Wednesday. Paloma sends a photo that afternoon of a tarp coming off a machine. Hi.

Good. That's what I'd want on my loop. A make or buy decision compares the full cost of each option over the quantity you need, leaves sunk costs out, and weighs capacity, expertise, and schedule. For a defined product with some cost risk, an incentive contract with a ceiling shares the risk and caps it.

Wednesday, February 8. Hana came to the change board with a proposal from the root cause team. The seat insert in the 7740 was a fluoropolymer, and two lots of it from 2058 had come from different batches of raw material. Nobody had ever compared them cold. Aldergrove's engineers wanted a materials lab to do it: six weeks and about $600,000.
Under the incentive fee task order, every dollar of it would be an allowable cost. The target cost had been $4.0 million since December.

Aldergrove's engineers had already asked the lab for a sample shipping kit. Garrett, at the end of the table, didn't see a problem. It's cost plus. Tell them to do it. That's the whole point of cost plus.
Hana looked at Sam. She'd been looking at him that way all week, as if she was about to say something else, and then not saying it.
Hana brings a $600,000 materials study, and Garrett says cost plus means just do it. How should Sam handle it?
A. Decline the study, and hold the task order to the scope fixed in December.
B. Tell Aldergrove to go ahead under the current task order, as an allowable root cause cost.
C. Let Hana approve the study as root cause lead, and have Peg file the modification afterward.
D. Take the study to the board as a change to the task order and reset its target first.

CR-0401 goes up the same afternoon: the study, its cost, its six weeks inside the root cause plan, what it might find, what it changes in the risk register. The board approves it. On Thursday Peg signs modification 2, raising the target cost to $4.6 million and the target fee with it, and leaving the fee floor and cap where they were, so the incentive still measures what it was built to measure. Quinn updates the plan. Aldergrove ships the samples on Friday. Nell sends Peg one line, copied to Sam. That's the first time in twenty six years anybody's changed a contract with us before the work instead of after.

Exactly right. Contract change control runs alongside the project's: assess the change at the board, then let the person with contracting authority modify the contract and adjust its terms, and update the plan, before the work begins.
Monday, February 13. Page eight came in the mail on a cold clear afternoon, green ink, Golden postmark. Sam read it at the kitchen table with the butter knife beside it and his coat still on.
0810 CALLED GARRITY BACK. TOLD HIM WE NEED IT ON THE 30TH. HE ASKED IF I'D LOOKED AT HIS ROW 3. TOLD HIM I'D LOOKED AT THE SCHEDULE.

He read the eight ten line four times, and the eight eleven line under it, THAT WAS TRUE, until it stopped being words. Then the line for April 30 at half past two. Filed the letter with the receiving papers. He'd sat across a table from Nell in her father's old office in December, and she'd told him about the drawer, and here was the other drawer.

The task order's first deliverable had her father's question in it, in Peg's words, badly punctuated. Nell had started calling Sam on Thursday afternoons, not about anything in particular, to tell him what the cold data said that week. Most weeks it said nothing yet. She called anyway.

The change board's minutes for December 7 had one line nobody had argued with: a member of Tallgrass's investor board chairs Kestrel Flow Controls, so any decision involving Kestrel comes to the board without Garrett's vote. Garrett had initialed it himself.

The board's clerk had acknowledged his note about the spare stacks in capitals and put the ARA's margin model on the March agenda. Sixty days of somebody's number would be argued about by people with badges, in public, which was where it belonged.

In Albuquerque the RP-55 line had made its first stack on February 6. Paloma had sent a photograph with her hand flat on the housing for scale. Rio Puerco's estimate at completion was 12.3 million, comfortably under the 13.5 million Peg had written on the file.

He made a list in the notebook of what had gone right since November, because Ray had told him once that a man who only lists his mistakes stops being able to see the rest. It was longer than he'd expected. He didn't trust it much.

Then he took the photocopy out of his briefcase, the one with STILL ASKING beside the third row, and put it in an envelope, and wrote Ruth's address in Golden on the front. He didn't seal it. He put it on the counter by the door, under his keys, where he'd see it every morning.

Friday, February 17. At 6:40 PM Hana Iwasaki was at his office door with her coat on and her car keys in her hand. She'd been there for a while before he looked up; he could tell from the way she was standing.
Can you come out to the stand? she said. Tonight. Just you. There's something I have to tell you, and I want to tell you out there.
He got his coat. On the way out they passed under the countdown clock, 366, and in the morning it would say 365. A year, exactly, and the wind coming up off the plains in the dark.
